sections.0.body.0.t: SCA (Software Composition Analysis) inventories the project's dependencies, direct and transitive, and cross-references each version with public vulnerability databases (NVD, GitHub Advisory, OSV) and license databases.

sections.0.body.1.t: The premise: most of the code in a modern application (often 70 to 90%) comes from third parties. Your risk surface includes all of it, even if nobody on the team wrote a line of those libraries.

sections.1.body.0.t: The starting point is always a manifest or lockfile. Say the project depends on an old version of lodash:

sections.1.heading.t: A real CVE: from lockfile to alert

sections.2.body.0.t: SCA takes each component+version from the lockfile and queries the vulnerability databases. For lodash 4.17.15, there is a real, well-known advisory:

sections.3.body.0.t: The case gets interesting when the vulnerable package is not even in your package.json: it came in as a dependency of a dependency, three levels down. You never chose that lodash, but it is in your artifact running in production.

sections.3.body.1.t: This is where the lockfile saves the day: it records the full tree, not just what is in the manifest. Without SCA and without a lockfile, the question 'do we use lodash 4.17.15?' has no quick answer, even in your own repository.

sections.3.heading.t: Why the transitive version is the nightmare

sections.4.bullets.0.t: reads manifests and lockfiles (package.json, package-lock, pom.xml, go.mod, requirements.txt)

sections.4.bullets.1.t: builds the full dependency tree, including transitive ones

sections.4.bullets.2.t: matches each component+version with published advisories and scores severity (CVSS, EPSS, known exploit)

sections.4.bullets.3.t: opens automatic update PRs and generates the artifact's SBOM

sections.5.body.0.t: On the PR and in the build, blocking new critical dependencies. And continuously after deploy: a new CVE against an old version appears every day. The tool monitors the inventory and alerts (or opens a PR) when an already-used dependency becomes a risk.

sections.5.heading.t: Where it fits in the pipeline

sections.6.bullets.0.t: only knows about already published vulnerabilities; a zero-day in a dependency gets through

sections.6.bullets.1.t: does not find flaws in your code: that is what SAST and DAST are for

sections.6.bullets.2.t: without a severity policy, it becomes a factory of ignored alerts

tagline.t: Watches the code you did not write: third-party libraries, versions and known vulnerabilities.
